code.title: Pool growth rules: core, queue, extra thread, reject

followUps:
Because it wants a hand-off, not a buffer: a SynchronousQueue has zero capacity, so offer succeeds only if an idle worker is already waiting to take the task.

Walk through the rules with core = 0. Rule 1 does not apply, so the pool offers the task to the queue. If an idle thread is parked in take, it receives the task and is reused. If none is idle, the offer fails at once and rule 3 starts a new thread. So the pool reuses idle threads and otherwise grows, up to Integer.MAX_VALUE. Idle threads die after 60 seconds.

Size it from the ratio of waiting time to working time, then confirm with load tests. A common formula is threads = cores x (1 + wait / compute).

Example: 8 cores, each request spends 90 ms waiting on a database and 10 ms on CPU. That gives 8 x (1 + 90/10) = 80 threads. CPU-bound work should use about cores (or cores + 1) instead. Then bound the queue, name the threads, and check the downstream limits: 80 threads are useless if the connection pool has 20 connections. Measure queue depth and p99 latency, and adjust.

It lets idle core threads time out and exit too, so the pool can shrink to zero threads when quiet. Normally core threads live forever.

It needs keepAliveTime > 0, otherwise it throws IllegalArgumentException. Example: core = 8, keepAlive = 30 s, allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). After 30 idle seconds all 8 threads end and no memory is held. The next task starts a thread again, at a small start-up cost. It is useful for rarely used pools such as a nightly batch helper. Call it before the pool is busy.

code.title: Unbounded queue in a fixed pool vs explicit bounds

followUps:
CallerRunsPolicy gives back-pressure: when the pool is saturated, the submitting thread runs the task itself, so it cannot submit more until that task finishes.

Example: a request thread submits tasks faster than 4 workers can finish them. Once the queue is full, each submit runs on the request thread, which slows the producer to the speed of the consumers. The downside is that the producer thread is busy and may block other work. AbortPolicy pushes the problem to the caller as an exception, which is also fine when you convert it to a 503. Discard policies hide the overload, so avoid them.

Watch the numbers that the pool already exposes: queue size, active threads, pool size, completed count and rejections, and alert when they stay high.

Read getQueue().size(), getActiveCount(), getPoolSize() and getLargestPoolSize(), and export them as metrics every few seconds. Saturation looks like this: active equals max, queue near capacity, rejections above zero, task wait time rising. Wrap tasks to record the time between submit and start (queue wait) and the run time. A thread dump showing all workers in the same blocking call tells you what they wait on.

code.title: Callable, Future and FutureTask with a captured exception

followUps:
cancel(true) marks the future as cancelled and, if the task is running, calls interrupt() on its thread. It does not forcibly stop it.

Details: if the task has not started, it will never run. If it is running, the worker thread's interrupt flag is set, and the task stops only if it checks the flag or calls a method such as sleep or wait that throws InterruptedException. A loop doing pure calculation ignores it. cancel(false) does not interrupt. After a successful cancel, get() throws CancellationException and isCancelled() is true. It returns false if the task already finished.

They let you inspect a finished future without catching checked exceptions. state() returns RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED, and resultNow() returns the value of a task that already succeeded.

Example: after invokeAll, loop over the futures: if f.state() == Future.State.SUCCESS use f.resultNow(); if FAILED, read f.exceptionNow(). If the task is not finished, resultNow() throws IllegalStateException, so it never blocks. That makes it handy for streams and for code that has already waited.

code.title: tryLock with timeout fails fast instead of blocking

followUps:
Barging means a thread that calls lock() can grab the lock the moment it is released, ahead of threads that have been waiting longer in the queue.

The default (non-fair) ReentrantLock allows it, and synchronized does too. It gives better throughput, because the running thread already has the cache warm and no thread switch is needed. The price is possible starvation of waiters. new ReentrantLock(true) hands the lock to the longest waiter, which is fairer but often several times slower. Use fair mode only after you actually measure starvation.

AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS) is the base class that manages a shared integer state and a queue of waiting threads. Most java.util.concurrent locks and synchronizers are built on it.

A subclass only decides what the state means and when tryAcquire or tryRelease succeeds. AQS does the rest: CAS on the state, queueing of threads that fail, parking and unparking them, and timeouts. In ReentrantLock the state is the hold count. In Semaphore it is the permits left. In CountDownLatch it is the remaining count.

In Java 24 (JEP 491) a virtual thread no longer gets pinned to its carrier when it blocks inside synchronized, so it unmounts like it does with a ReentrantLock.

In Java 21 to 23, blocking on I/O or wait inside a synchronized block kept the carrier thread stuck, and with few carriers this could stall everything. The advice was to switch such code to ReentrantLock. On 24 and later that rewrite is no longer needed. Pinning can still happen when the stack contains a native frame.

code.title: ReadWriteLock downgrade works, upgrade does not

followUps:
validate(stamp) tells you whether a write lock was taken since you got the stamp, i.e. whether the data you read optimistically is still consistent.

Pattern: long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead(); double x = this.x, y = this.y; if (!sl.validate(s)) { s = sl.readLock(); try { x = this.x; y = this.y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); } }. The optimistic read takes no lock and writes no shared state, so it is very cheap. If a writer got in between, validate returns false and you retry with a real read lock. You must copy the fields to locals first and only use them after a successful validate.

Keep the config in an immutable object and store it in a volatile field or AtomicReference. Readers just read the reference; the writer builds a new object and swaps it.

volatile Config cfg = new Config(...);
Config c = cfg;            // readers: one volatile read
void update(Config n) { cfg = n; }  // writer: replace whole snapshot

Readers always see one consistent version, never a half-updated one, and never block. The cost is allocating a new object per update, which is fine for config that changes rarely. Use compareAndSet if several writers derive the new value from the old one.

code.title: Latch, semaphore and barrier in one demo

followUps:
The worker's countDown() never runs, so the latch count never reaches zero and every thread waiting in await() hangs forever.

Example: new CountDownLatch(3) and one of three workers throws before countDown. The count stays at 1. Fix: call countDown() in a finally block, and in the waiter use await(timeout, unit) so a failure becomes a visible timeout. Remember that the latch is one-shot: it cannot be reset once at zero.

Because a barrier needs all parties running at the same time, and a pool with fewer threads than parties can never get them all to await() together.

Example: CyclicBarrier(4) with tasks in a pool of 2 threads. Two tasks reach the barrier and block, taking both threads, so tasks 3 and 4 stay in the queue and never run. The barrier never trips. Make the pool at least as large as the parties (and not shared with other blocking work), or use virtual threads. A timeout on await turns the hang into a BrokenBarrierException.

code.title: CAS retry loop with atomic counters

followUps:
On x86 the JVM compiles incrementAndGet to a single LOCK XADD instruction, which adds and returns the old value atomically, so no retry loop is needed.

A generic CAS loop reads, adds one, and tries CMPXCHG; if another core won, it repeats. XADD always succeeds on the first try, because the hardware locks the cache line during the add. So under contention it is faster than a loop, with fewer wasted attempts. Other operations such as compareAndSet still use LOCK CMPXCHG. This is a JIT intrinsic and an implementation detail, so the semantics stay the same on other CPUs.

False sharing is when two threads write to different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line (usually 64 bytes), so the line bounces between cores even though the data is unrelated.

Example: two threads each increment their own long, but the two fields are neighbours. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, and the loop can run several times slower than with separate lines. @Contended (internal, enabled with -XX:-RestrictContended) makes the JVM pad the field to its own cache line. LongAdder uses it for its cells. The price is wasted memory, so use it only on proven hot fields.

code.title: ABA: plain CAS misses it, stamped reference catches it

followUps:
No. The GC removes ABA caused by memory reuse of a freed node, but not ABA caused by your own code putting the same object back.

While thread 1 holds a reference to node A, the GC cannot free A, so no new object can reuse its address. But if thread 2 pops A and later pushes the same A object again (for example from an object pool or a cache), the CAS sees the same reference and succeeds although the state in between changed. So pooling nodes brings the problem back. Allocating a fresh node for every push, or using a stamp, avoids it.

AtomicMarkableReference pairs a reference with one boolean mark, updated atomically together. It is used to flag a node as logically deleted.

In a lock-free linked list, deleting node X is done in two steps: first CAS the mark on X's next pointer to true (logically deleted), then unlink it. Because the mark and the pointer change in one CAS, nobody can insert after a node that is being deleted. This is the core idea of Harris's lock-free list, and of ConcurrentSkipListMap style structures. It is cheaper than a full stamp when you need only one bit.

code.title: Bounded producer-consumer with poison pill and shedding

followUps:
With wait/notify, notify wakes just one waiting thread, which may be the wrong kind (a producer waking a producer), so the signal is lost and everything can stall. notifyAll wakes everyone and each rechecks its condition.

Example: a queue of size 1 with 2 producers and 2 consumers all in the same wait set. A consumer takes an item and calls notify; it wakes the other consumer, which finds the queue empty and waits again. Now both producers are still asleep and nobody makes progress. Use a while loop around wait, and notifyAll, or use two Condition objects (notFull, notEmpty) with signal.

Route all items with the same key to the same single consumer, for example by hash(key) % N picking one of N queues, each with its own consumer thread.

Example: N = 4 queues, user 17 maps to queue 1, so all events for user 17 are processed in order by consumer 1, while other users run in parallel on the other three. Do not put all consumers on one queue and expect order, because two consumers can finish out of order. Kafka does the same with partitions chosen by key. A hot key then limits throughput to one consumer, which is the cost of ordering.

code.title: thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine

followUps:
Because failure propagates down the chain: stages after a failed stage are skipped, and an error stays an error until some stage recovers it with exceptionally, handle or similar.

Example: supplyAsync(A).thenApply(B).thenApply(C). If A throws, B and C never run, and the final future completes with a CompletionException that wraps the original exception. Calling get() wraps it in ExecutionException. Place exceptionally right after the risky stage to continue with a fallback, or at the end to handle any failure.

Usually not. cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture only completes that future with CancellationException; the interrupt flag has no effect on it.

CompletableFuture is not tied to a thread, so there is nothing to interrupt. The task started with supplyAsync keeps running and its result is dropped. Downstream stages see a CancellationException (wrapped as CompletionException). To really stop work, check a shared flag or keep the Future of the executor task and cancel that, or design the task to look at isCancelled().

code.title: Error recovery and timeouts in CompletableFuture

followUps:
join() throws the unchecked CompletionException, while get() throws the checked ExecutionException (plus InterruptedException). Both hold the real error in getCause().

Example: the task throws IOException. get() gives ExecutionException with cause IOException; join() gives CompletionException with the same cause. join() is easier inside lambdas and streams because nothing is checked, and it cannot be interrupted. get(timeout, unit) exists for waiting a bounded time; with join use orTimeout. If the future was cancelled, both throw CancellationException.

Retry by wrapping the call in a method that, on failure, schedules the next attempt after a growing delay, and stops after a maximum number of tries.

CompletableFuture<T> retry(Supplier<CompletableFuture<T>> call, int left, long delayMs) {
  return call.get().exceptionallyCompose(ex -> left == 0 ? CompletableFuture.failedFuture(ex)
    : CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> null, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(delayMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))
        .thenCompose(x -> retry(call, left - 1, delayMs * 2)));
}

Delays 100, 200, 400 ms double each time. Add random jitter so many clients do not retry together, and retry only errors that can succeed later.

code.title: 10,000 virtual threads with blocking sleeps

followUps:
Pinning is when a virtual thread is stuck to its carrier thread while blocked, so the carrier cannot run other virtual threads. This wastes the cheap-thread advantage.

In Java 21 to 23 it happens when blocking inside a synchronized block, or when a native method or foreign call is on the stack. Detect it with the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, or run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full to print a stack trace when it happens. Fix by using ReentrantLock for blocking sections or by moving to Java 24+, where synchronized no longer pins.

Both tools make concurrent code easier to follow, and they pair well with cheap threads: StructuredTaskScope manages a group of subtasks, and ScopedValue passes read-only data to them.

StructuredTaskScope (preview) forks each subtask in its own virtual thread and joins them in one place, so a failure can cancel the siblings and no thread outlives the block. ScopedValue is an immutable value bound for the duration of a block and inherited by forked subtasks. Compared with ThreadLocal it is lighter, cannot be changed by callees, and is cleaned up automatically, which suits millions of virtual threads.

code.title: Semaphore caps concurrency of virtual threads

followUps:
Put a limit in front of each downstream with a Semaphore (a bulkhead), so only N calls are in flight and the rest wait or fail fast.

Semaphore db = new Semaphore(20);
if (!db.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new Busy();
try { return query(); } finally { db.release(); }

Set N to what the dependency can handle, for example the DB connection pool size of 20. Virtual threads that wait on the semaphore cost almost nothing. The timeout turns overload into a quick error instead of a long queue. Add a metric for permit wait time so you can see it.

Roll back when measurements show virtual threads are not helping or are hurting, and you cannot fix the cause quickly: for example CPU-bound handlers, heavy pinning on Java 21 from a library you cannot change, or a native driver that blocks carriers.

Run a canary: send 5% of traffic to the new version and compare p99 latency, error rate, CPU and DB wait. If p99 is worse by more than your budget and JFR shows pinning or saturation you cannot remove this week, switch back to a bounded platform pool through the feature flag. Keep the virtual-thread version behind the flag so you can retry later after the fix.

code.title: Thread-starvation deadlock in a one-thread pool and its fix

followUps:
ForkJoinPool.join() does not just block: while the task is not done, the waiting worker runs other queued tasks (work stealing), so it stays useful and a child task can run on the same thread.

Example: a parent splits into two children with fork(). When it calls left.join() and the left child is still unstarted in its own deque, the parent pops and runs it directly. If the child was stolen, the worker may help with other tasks, or the pool adds a spare thread through the managed blocker. This is why recursive divide-and-conquer works with a small pool without starving.

A thread dump shows every pool thread parked in Future.get (or CompletableFuture.join), with the stack going through your task code, while the queue still holds waiting tasks.

Take dumps with jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print a few seconds apart. Signs: all workers named pool-1-thread-N are in WAITING in FutureTask.awaitDone, no thread is running a child task, and the same stacks repeat in each dump. There are no lock owners, so the dump does not report a deadlock, and you must recognise this pattern yourself. Check the pool's queue size to confirm.
